title: Plea before Telangana High Court seeks publication of 1.16 lakh unpublished government orders
summary: A plea has been filed before the Telangana High Court alleging that the State government has failed to make public over 1.16 lakh Government Orders (GOs) issued since June 2014 despite earlier court directions to upload them online [B Vinay Reddy v The State of Telangana & Ors.].Filed by one B Vinay Reddy, the petition claims that the State government had informed the Telangana Legislative Assembly in March 2025 that 1,99,115 GOs had been issued between June 2, 2014 and March 14, 2025, of which only 82,657 were available in the public domain. As per the plea, 1,16,458 GOs or around 58.5 per cent are not publicly accessible.A subsequent response to an RTI application, dated November 18, 2025, showed that only 3,290 of the 19,064 GOs issued between December 7, 2023 and January 26, 2025 were available in the public domain.The plea is pending before Justice Surepalli Nanda.Justice Surepalli NandaThe plea alleges that the State government departments classify GOs as either 'public' or 'internal' on the Government Order Issue Register (GOIR) portal. It contends that departments withhold GOs without issuing reasoned orders citing Sections 8 or 9 of the RTI Act, which specify grounds for denying access to information. The petition argues that this practice prevents citizens from accessing government decisions that may affect their rights.As per the plea,“A Government Order which is kept out of the public domain cannot be known, obeyed, questioned or relied upon by the citizen whose rights it affects." The plea also refers to two earlier High Court orders passed on March 10, 2022 and December 23, 2025, directing the State to upload unpublished GOs within eight weeks. The petition submits that the directions have not been fully implemented.A contempt of court case concerning alleged non-compliance is also pending before the Court.The petitioner has sought directions from the High Court to the State government to publish all GOs issued since June 2, 2014, except those withheld for legally valid reasons. It also seeks disclosure of department-wise figures on unpublished orders, deadlines for uploading future orders and appointment of officers responsible for publishing them.The plea also challenges delays in responding to Reddy’s Right to Information (RTI) application filed on January 17, 2026, seeking year-wise and department-wise details of GOs issued and uploaded since 2014, reasons for non-publication and the rules governing it. The plea further alleges that the Telangana Information Commission took up Reddy's complaint, filed on February 22, only on July 15. It was heard three times without a decision and adjourned on October 13 without a next date being fixed. The petition also claims that the Commission had failed to provide hearing records or facilitate video-conference participation.“A body created to enforce transparency cannot withhold from a party the record of his own proceeding,” states the plea.The petition seeks directions to provide the requested RTI information free of cost within two weeks and decide his pending complaint within four weeks. It also seeks hybrid hearings, at least seven days’ advance notice of hearing dates and uploading of hearing records within three days.The plea was filed through advocate Mahesh Mamindla.

title: Delhi High Court rejects plea by Neha Bora against notice to sign bond and "maintain peace"
summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday dismissed a plea filed by All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora challenging a notice issued the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) directing Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 and maintain peace.Justice Subramonium Prasad passed the order."Writ petition is rejected. However, there are certain directions give for the magistrate to take care of. All the material to be furnished to her," the Court said.The Court added that the magistrate [SEM] will also consider the import of Section 135 BNSS. “Whether 135 would warrant a production of the bond at the very first instance, or it's only during the course of the inquiries, and further incident take place, which gives the danger or not. These are matters the magistrate will take into account,” the court said.Justice Subramonium PrasadThe notice under challenge was issued by the Delhi Police to Bora on October 18, directing them to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) on October 19. It directed Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 with a surety to “maintain peace during the period of inquiry” against them.According to Bora’s plea, the notice dated October 17 was issued by the SEM under Sections 126 and 130, read with Section 135(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), citing apprehensions of breach of public peace and tranquillity.Bora was detained on October 16 while attending a gathering at Mandi House. Bora alleged that they were taken to an undisclosed location and subsequently to RK Puram police station, where they were held overnight before being released at 6 AM the following day. They received the SEM notice on October 18.The notice cited allegations of sloganeering at Mandi House, repeated protests around Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and allegedly instigating people to participate in a protest at Connaught Place.However, according to Bora's plea, the notice does not disclose any material establishing a likelihood of breach of peace or identify a specific event or period during which such a breach is apprehended.The petition also disputed the allegation concerning the Connaught Place protest. Bora argued that their call was for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5 pm on October 16, where they were subsequently detained.Bora alleged that the proceedings amount to an attempt to curb peaceful dissent and violate their fundamental rights to freedom of speech, assembly and personal liberty.Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for Bora, submitted that all calls made by them were for peaceful protests."The facts are that over a period of time certain protests have arisen in the country as it the want against what the government does. As far as my client is concerned there has been no exhortation to violence it has been entirely peaceful. She has been asking for reforms. Over time, she has put out tweets and exhorted people to join," it was submitted.Sankaranarayanan referred to the press conference held by Bora on October 15 in response to the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site.He sought to distinguish the protest that happened at Connaught Place from the one which Bora had called for at Mandi House.Sankaranarayanan added that there is nothing wrong in making a call for a regime change in a democracy. Senior Advocate Gopal SankaranarayananHe also highlighted how the special executive magistrate issuing the notice is also a police officer."It is admitted that there was a direction by senior officers to initiate the procedure under Section 126. It is relevant because the SEM here is also an ACP," it was pointed out.He further flagged errors in the notice and maintained that no permission is required to hoist the national flag.Neha Bora No permission is needed to hoist the national flag.Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma, appearing for Delhi Police, rebutted Bora's arguments. The ASG said that Section 126 and 130 of the BNSS have to be read together."If there is a likelihood that somebody may commit breach of peace, Section 126 BNSS kicks in with Section 130 BNSS. They can't be disjoined. Such technical splitting will take away the essence of public tranquillity and breach of peace," the ASG contended.ASG Chetan SharmaASG Sharma maintained that the notice was based on likelihood of breach of peace and cannot be assailed on the ground of technicality."Don't leave it to a technicality... All mayhem may have broken loose in the capital of the city. Because this is preventive in nature so that law would land its weight to the way parliament envisaged it to be," the ASG argued.Regarding Bora's arguments that the notice was factually incorrect since she was had not given any call for protest at Connaught Place but only at Mandi House, the ASG said,"Their argument that their call was only for Mandi House and not CP and that no 163 BNSS was in force is false. There was 163 BNSS. Police was outnumbered, she ran. She dodges. She was stopped, she did not stop. She ran towards CP."Besides Sankaranarayanan, advocates Abhik Chimni, Moksha Sharma, Ayan Dasgupta Samarendra, Pranjal Abrol and Gurupal Singh also appeared for Bora.ASG Chetan Sharma and CGSC Ashish Dixit represented the Delhi Police.

title: Legal tech in law firms and in-house teams: The wall is coming down
summary: For years, the legal technology market organised itself in a peculiar way. Law firms on one side, in-house legal teams on the other. Both bought legal tech, but rarely the same products. Legal research, document management and eDiscovery crossed over. Almost everything else split; the platforms were built around workflows pointing in opposite directions.The split made sense, because the two sides were buying for different outcomes. A firm sells expert time to external clients, so its technology existed to capture that time and protect the margin on it. Success meant utilisation and realisation. An in-house team is a business-enabler with one client - the business - and an ever-increasing queue of internal requests. The outcome it needs is the business moving safely with high velocity with as few lawyer hours as possible. Its work also doesn't end at signing: obligations and renewals run on for years. So technology that focuses on this side historically existed to route the volume and keep track of what happens after the deal closes.Firm tech made expert hours more valuable, whereas in-house tech aimed to make fewer of those hours necessary.That split is now breaking at one layer and hardening at another. The models are shared. The products built on them are starting to split again along the old line.The frontier model broke the wall (before vendors acted on it) Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT are used by law firms and in-house teams alike, often through enterprise deployments with no legal-specific wrapper. A partner drafting a memo and a general counsel stress-testing a contract position can be working in the same model, through the same interface. This matters because previous generations of legal technology were integration plays. They connected existing workflows, automated document flows and surfaced existing data in more useful formats. The intelligence, such as it was, lived mostly in the rules and structured data that humans had built around the system. The model itself was not the product. But that is changing. Frontier models can take on work that used to need a lawyer at every step. Of course, the output still needs real oversight, but it doesn't need rebuilding from scratch. When the same capability serves an associate and in-house counsel doing comparable work, the case for two separate product markets gets thin.But what about the core legaltech vendors? This play is most visible at the platform layer. Harvey launched as a law firm tool and is now a fixture in in-house environments. Luminance built its reputation in law firm due diligence and has expanded steadily into CLM and legal operations. Legora sells one platform to both, but is now building segment-specific products on top of it. The companies themselves rarely frame this as convergence; they frame it as expansion.This is partly commercial. Law firms and in-house teams are both large buyers and serving only one side of the relationship is a constraint, not a strategy. But it is also a product decision, because the underlying tasks are not as different as the market structure implied. Contract analysis looks similar whether the lawyer doing it sits in a firm or a legal department. So does due diligence, drafting, regulatory review, issue spotting. The divide was shrinking before the legal tech vendors had fully registered it.Shared engine, separate front doors The legal AI tools may be shared, but how law firms and in-house departments use it in their workflows are completely different.Law firms operate around matters: defined engagements with starts, ends, billing codes and client reporting. In-house legal teams operate around continuous flows of work with no natural beginning, internal stakeholders instead of paying clients and obligations that run across time rather than project. These are not just organisational differences. They reflect genuinely different ways of thinking about how legal work is structured.An in-house team using a platform built around matter logic will encounter assumptions that do not map onto how their work flows. A law firm using a platform built around operational throughput will find itself reaching for structures the product did not anticipate. Capability has converged faster than workflow design has. The platforms are still working out what a genuinely shared model of legal work looks like when you are not starting from an assumption about which institutional context it sits inside.October 2026 showed how vendors are answering that. In the same week, Legora and Harvey each launched a product called Intake. Each is a front door for in-house teams that captures requests, asks for missing context, routes work to the right lawyer and drafts a first pass from the team’s own playbooks. Legora’s is live in Slack. Harvey’s is in early access. Both are built for legal departments, not firms. The engine is shared and the product on top of it is splitting along the old line. None of this is new. The previous generation of legal tech didn't just segment the market, but encoded the split. Firms bought practice management and billing built around engagements with a paying client. Legal departments bought the mirror image: matter management and e-billing built to control spend on those same engagements. Same matter, opposite ends of the invoice.CLM’s problem is that the AI platforms are coming in-house Contract lifecycle management (CLM) is the clearest case. These systems were built entirely around in-house legal operations: intake portals, approval workflows, obligation tracking, renewal calendars. Law firms have no native use of CLM, but at times offer it as a managed service to clients.For years, the threat to CLM vendors looked distant, because legal AI platforms were law firm tools. That’s no longer true. The platforms that won the firms are now selling directly to legal departments and they’re taking pieces of the CLM stack with them. Take contract redlining. A firm associate reviewing a counterparty's MSA and an in-house counsel handling an incoming NDA can each load a playbook and fallback positions into Spellbook or Harvey inside Word and get speedy redlines, with comments explaining each change. The only difference is whose playbook it is. For the firm, it belongs to the client and for the in-house team, it belongs to the company.Obligation tracking follows the same pattern through tabular extraction. A firm running diligence on a deal and a legal department auditing its own executed agreements can both drop a batch of contracts into Harvey Vault or Legora's Tabular Review. Each gets a grid with one row per contract and columns for renewal dates, notice periods, payment terms and audit rights.Intake goes further. Harvey’s version routes contract work into its own Contract Intelligence product. That looks less like a workaround to CLM and more like a bid to become it.The legacy vendors built their moats around the assumption that the two markets would stay separate. Legal AI platforms are making that assumption look increasingly fragile.Clients now know what the work takes Firms have long operated on the basis that they knew what work required what expertise, how long it took and what it was worth. Clients accepted that framing because they lacked a credible alternative. An in-house team using the same platform as their outside counsel starts to develop real intuitions about how long document review should take, what contract analysis actually involves and where human judgment adds value versus where it is reconstructing work the platform could have done faster. Those intuitions enter conversations about scope, budgets and billing. They change what clients feel entitled to ask.The bigger shift is in information, more than fees. When both parties in a professional services relationship are working within the same technological frame, the knowledge gap that historically structured that relationship starts to close. What gets renegotiated is not just cost. It is the definition of the service itself.Nobody has worked out how juniors learn to supervise The law firm model has always depended on a specific learning architecture. Junior lawyers do structured work - research, drafting, review - and develop judgment through repetition and feedback. That judgment eventually becomes what clients pay senior rates for. It works because the early work is meaningful in both output and developmental terms.If a platform handles first-pass contract review as well as a junior associate, the question is not just what the associate does instead. It is how the associate develops the judgment to supervise and refine the platform's work without having done the underlying task enough times to know what it feels like to get it wrong. Supervision without prior experience is a different skill and the profession has not yet worked out how to build it.In-house teams face an adjacent version and it’s no longer hypothetical. Legora’s Intake can complete pre-approved routine requests end-to-end and send the answer straight back to the business. Harvey’s platform resolves routine requests and drafts the rest. A lawyer reviewing that output is working on what to remove from the material. That’s often efficient. It can also slowly wear away the close engagement that makes oversight mean something. The risk is that lawyers stop knowing what they’re looking for.Accountability has not caught up with the platforms Traditional legal technology came with a defined responsibility map. The vendor supplied the tool, the organisation implemented it and the lawyer remained professionally accountable for the work product. That held because the tool was doing something discrete and bounded: retrieving a document, surfacing a clause, flagging a deadline.Platforms operating across both environments are doing something more continuous. They shape how work is initiated, scoped, analysed and delivered. The lawyer remains accountable, but the platform is increasingly embedded in the chain of decisions that leads to the output the lawyer signs off on. When something goes wrong, the question of where the error entered the process is genuinely difficult to answer. The legal profession has governance frameworks developed over a very long time for very good reasons. The question is not whether they apply here. It is what they look like when the assistance is this deeply embedded in the work itself.The wall was never natural and it’s being rebuilt The fault line that organised the legal technology market for decades was never natural. It was a product of how technology was built, how professional services relationships were structured and how the economics of legal work had historically developed. None of that was permanent. It was contingent.What the current generation of Legal AI platforms is doing, more than anything else, is making that contingency visible. The harder questions - who captures the value that gets displaced, how expertise develops in this new architecture, where professional accountability sits when a platform is this embedded in legal work - are not going to be resolved by the technology itself. They require the profession to make active choices about what it is actually for.Those conversations are beginning, but they're running well behind what's shifting. The sharpest one: if clients learn what the work takes and juniors stop doing it, who gets paid for the judgment that's left? Shreya Vajpei is the Founder of Indian LegalTech Network.Vaishali Gopal is Senior Advisor, Indian LegalTech Network and Founder of Future Relics Consulting.

title: SEM notice asking Neha Bora to sign peace bond not based on mere hearsay: Delhi High Court
summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday observed that the show-cause notice issued by a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) to All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 and maintain peace was not based on mere "hearsay". Justice Subramonium Prasad observed that the notice was based on the kalandara dated October 17, which consists of the three general diary entries registered at different police stations related to different dates and events. "As such, this Court cannot sit in the armchair of the SEM to test the subjective satisfaction of the sufficiency of material and as to whether the opinion has been correctly been arrived at by the SEM or not," the Bench said. The Court said that the notice, issued under Sections 126 and 130 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), met the legal requirements for initiating preventive proceedings.The High Court arrived at these findings while dismissing Bora's plea against the notice. However, the Court directed the police to provide all the material to Bora on which reliance will be placed at the time of enquiry and on which basis the notice has been issued. "The SEM is also directed to ensure that the principles of natural justice are not violated before passing any order directing furnishing of a bond," the Court ordered. It clarified that the SEM must independently assess the material before deciding whether Bora should be directed to furnish a bond during the inquiry. "This Court, however, deems it fit to state that the SEM must necessarily keep in mind the import of Section 135 of the BNSS and leaves it open for the SEM to decide on the insistence of a bond at the first instance, as the provision provides for furnishing a bond only if there is an apprehension of breach of peace or disturbance after the commencement and before the completion of the enquiry," the Court said. Justice Subramonium PrasadThe notice under challenge was issued by the Delhi Police to Bora on October 18, directing them to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) on October 19. title: Legal Notes by Arvind Datar: Tea with 103-year-old Taraporevala
summary: On October 22, 2026, I had the privilege of having tea with 103-year-old Vicaji J. Taraporevala. I have known this centenarian for almost three decades but was meeting him after 20 years.I shall always be grateful to Justice Manoj Sanklecha, retired judge of the Bombay High Court, and Taraporevala’s former junior, for arranging this meeting. For some inexplicable reason, Justice Sanklecha’s number appeared on my phone’s screen on October 21. By a happy coincidence, I was to appear before the Bombay High Court the next day. I called him and enquired about Taraporevala. To my delight, I was told that he was fine. Justice Sanklecha agreed to fix an appointment the next evening.Justice Manoj Sanklecha, Vicaji J TaraporevalaMy mind went down memory lane. There was a case before the Customs and Excise Tribunal, and Taraporevala was unable to come down to Chennai. Sanklecha and I appeared and we succeeded. Thereafter, I remained in touch with Taraporevala for some time.Early daysVicaji Jivanji Taraporewala was born on June 21, 1923 and joined the chambers of the leading Sir Jamshedji Kanga in 1946. (Incidentally, Nani Palkhivala had joined the same chamber two years earlier). Over the years, Taraporevala practised before the Supreme Court, the Bombay High Court and, particularly, before the Central Excise, Customs and Service Tax Tribunal (CESTAT).Renowned authorWhat set Taraporevala apart from other lawyers were his legal commentaries. Well before I had the opportunity of working with him, I had purchased his excellent commentary on the “Law of Central Excise”. This branch became an important area of practice in the late 70s as every manufactured product became liable to excise duty. In 1982, the Tribunal was formed with a Principal Bench in New Delhi and four regional benches. I had to often refer to Taraporevala’s commentary on this subject and was impressed with his explanation of the basic concepts of this levy. The success of this book encouraged him to write another commentary on “Customs law – Custom Levy, Valuation and Classification”. This too became an indispensable book for indirect tax practitioners.In 2005, my bookseller brought me a copy of Law of Intellectual Property. To my surprise, it was written by Taraporevala. This book was released when he was 82 years old, and its popularity called for two further editions in 2012 and 2019. It is very rare indeed for a lawyer to write a commentary on completely diverse topics.But a bigger surprise was in store for me when I met him for tea two days ago. His son told me that his first book was published in 1963, titled Medical Law and Ethics in India, and co-authored with Dr Homi Shapurji Mehta.After having practiced for five decades, Taraporevala started losing his hearing ability and turned increasingly to writing and wrote a few more books. His vast experience in the legal profession led him to write “Tales from the Bench and Bar”. This book has captured the experience, traditions and professional life of the legal community and has been published in three editions. His love for literature led him to write “Lilting and Eloquent English: A Symphony of Words”. This book examines the distinctive quality of celebrated writers Shakespeare, Oliver Goldsmith and Rudyard Kipling. This is the first part of the book, and the second part examines the eloquent speeches that were made in the context of freedom, democracy, patriotism and political leadership.Vicaji J TaraporevalaI was amazed to learn that he obtained special permission from the then Chief Justice Mohit Shah to use the Judges' library when he pursued his research from 2012 to 2022. This means that he went to the library every day from the age of 89 to 99! At the age of 102, he published a commentary on “Administrative Law”, with Dr. Uma Narayan as the co-author. She was the former Deputy Registrar of the Bombay High Court and also the Registrar of the Supreme Court of India, and is now an advocate at the Bombay High Court. This 250-page book admirably summarises the essential principles of administrative law. At 103, he is now writing another book that relates to English Literature!!Personal life: Taraporevala, in his earlier days, was fairly disciplined. He ate frugally, is a teetotaller and swam every day. Today, he walks every evening in his apartment complex. But he does not follow any specific diet. I was both delighted and amazed to see him eating two onion pakodas and a Coke, while Sanklecha and I had pakodas and Tea. What is even more remarkable is that Taraporevala is a cancer survivor and had a major surgery in 2008. But this did not slow him down, and 18 years later, he is still writing. Such grit and determination is an inspiration to all of us. Taraporevala lost his wife just two years ago, and she was ten years younger than him. His son, Kai, worked in the petroleum sector and later went on to the financial services sector. After retirement, he now takes care of his father. Kai is also an author of books on diverse topics – the latest book is titled “From Prehistory to the Age of AGI” Taraporevala’s daughter lives in New Zealand.Chair used by J. D. InverarityTaraporevala’s flat has a small piece but important piece of history: a chair used by the legendary J.D. Inverarity. In his autobiography, Roses in December, Justice Chagla mentions that John Duncan Inverarity was the leader of the Bombay Bar, and Chapter Four contains anecdotes about this English lawyer. The chair used by Inverarity is now possessed by Taraporevala.All good things must come to an end. The evening spent with him, Justice Sanklecha and his son will always be remembered by me. While leaving, he insisted that I should meet him again on my next visit to Bombay High Court and I intend to do just that.Arvind Datar is a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of India.The author gratefully acknowledges the assistance of Dr. Uma Narayan, Advocate in the writing of this article

title: Reservation for converts: The unsettled question of substantive equality
summary: While upholding a Madras High Court verdict, the Supreme Court found that conversion to Islam alone does not entitle a person to a seat in any of the seven Muslim communities declared as backward classes (BCs) by the Tamil Nadu government.The case began when Paramasivam (Sameer Ahmed after conversion), a resident of Thoothukudi district in Tamil Nadu, converted from Hinduism to Islam in 2015 and sought to be recognised as a member of one of the Muslim communities listed as backward classes by the State government. Authorities rejected his application for a community certificate. Challenging this decision, Paramasivam approached the Madras High Court, which declared the Tamil Nadu government's government order, allowing a person who converted to Islam from BC, MBC, DC, or SC to be treated as BC (Muslim), unconstitutional. The Tamil Nadu government then appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court.A Bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Sri Chandrasekhar formulated the precise question: whether a person belonging to a BC, MBC, DC, or SC prior to such conversion can, after embracing Islam, claim the status and consequential benefits of a BC Muslim.In its reasoning, the Court emphasised that a person converting from the Hindu social order to a non-Hindu social order cannot claim affirmative action under Article 16(4) of the Constitution merely because of the social backwardness associated with their pre-conversion status. A community certificate is issued based on established lineage and social status within the specified backward classes, not merely based on religious conversion. The judges also referred to previous Supreme Court decisions holding that determining social and educational backwardness under Article 16(4) of the Constitution must consider an individual's status within a recognised community, not just a change in religion. Thus, without proof of acceptance into the specific backward class Muslim community, a convert cannot automatically claim reservation benefits accorded to that group.This verdict goes beyond a legal battle over a community certificate and raises several important debates in our society. Central among these are questions of identity. If a person leaves one religious community but is not automatically accepted into every social group associated with the new religion, where does that leave the person socially and legally? For example, if a person from SC who benefited from reservation converts and embraces Islam, but cannot claim community membership to any of the recognised communities within Islam that actually enjoy reservation, what will become of him? These questions no longer concern religious identity, but social identity and its legal recognition.Does conversion immediately end one’s social backwardness? Conversion may not instantly remove the effects of historical discrimination, as social stigma and disadvantage can persist regardless of a change in religion.In the Chinthada Anand case, the appellant was a Christian pastor who claimed he belonged to the Madiga community, a Scheduled Caste, and was abused by referring to his caste. It was argued that caste is a matter of birth and not of faith, and a change of religion does not wipe out the social identity and historical disadvantages attached to one’s caste. The Supreme Court had dismissed the appeal observing that "the appellant converted to Christianity, the caste status, which he earlier enjoyed as a member of the Madiga community, stood eclipsed in the eyes of law". The appellant thus could not invoke the protections of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (SC/ST) Act.In CM Arumugam’s case, it was held that "once such a person ceases to be a Hindu and becomes a Christian, the social and economic disabilities arising because of the Hindu religion cease, and hence it is no longer necessary to give him protection, and for this reason he is deemed not to belong to a scheduled caste".Although in practice, both Islam and Christianity were prone to a hierarchical social structure similar to caste, theologically, they do not have any inherent superior and inferior social structure. This distinction is crucial. Indra Sawhney’s case rightly recognised this. The nine-judge bench in that case observed that "among non-Hindus, several occupational groups, sects, and denominations are, for historical reasons, socially backward. They too represent backward social collectivities for the purposes of Article 16(4)". Therefore, it seems logical that a person converting to such religions cannot carry past social disadvantages with them.In the present case, the Court went a step further and acknowledged that at times, past social disadvantages follow a person when they convert to a different religion. Interestingly, the Court held that even if past social disadvantage follows, it still cannot be a ground for availing reservation benefits. It then explained the basis for this distinction. The reason is that social backwardness is treated as a condition arising from membership in a particular social structure whose foundational basis is caste. This is a crucial difference and a slight shift from previous decisions.Earlier, the Supreme Court in Soosai v. Union of India, placed the responsibility on Christian converts to prove that they still face caste discrimination despite changing their religion. Similarly, in S Anbalagan’s case, the Court acknowledged that a person who belongs to a caste does not automatically lose their caste status upon conversion to Christianity. Since the petitioner has reconverted to Hinduism and was accepted as a member of the Scheduled Caste community throughout his life, he was fully qualified to contest elections from a constituency reserved for Scheduled Castes.In G Michael’s case, the Madras High Court held that as a general rule, conversion operates as an expulsion from the caste; in other words, a convert ceases to have any caste.In the present case, the Court concluded that a person's former caste position alone cannot establish membership in a backward class associated with the person's new religion that is not theologically based on caste. The Court recognised the petitioner's religious identity but declined to recognise the petitioner’s social identity and thus denied it legal recognition.The Court’s observation above seems to miss a crucial point. When the Court acknowledges that social disadvantage follows a converted person, it becomes a social reality and that social reality need not necessarily emanate from caste or be backed by theological scriptures. Caste is, in essence, a socially constructed reality in its mechanism and a theologically backed social structure in its continuation and enforcement. Therefore, when caste becomes social reality, it has consequences in a non-Hindu social order. Even if a converted person wants to detach himself from this social reality, he cannot. And when he does, he faces consequences for that detachment. In the book titled Karukku, the author Bama explores how caste penetrated Christianity. Nothing has changed, she concludes. Investigative reports such as the Hindu's video report on caste discrimination in Christianity highlight how caste hierarchies continue to manifest within church institutions and social practices in Tamil Nadu.Another crucial difference appears in the present case. The petitioner sought to join one of the seven Muslim communities identified as backward by the Tamil Nadu government. This is why the Supreme Court distinguished between being a member of a religion and being a member of a particular community within that religion. If a person converts to Islam, he effectively steps out of the community in which he was born and enters into a religion that has different social communities that are categorised as backwards by the government. Therefore, one cannot seek membership in the different communities within that religion, nor can one claim reservation benefits by converting to it. Thus, even if a person converted to Islam suffers social and educational backwardness, he cannot claim reservation, because being a member of a particular community in the host religion is by established lineage.Where does this person stand? Let’s assume that a person is converting to Islam for want of dignity, equal treatment and equal respect or any other religion for that matter. He may get them, but the conversion cannot ameliorate his social and educational backwardness because such social disadvantages prima facie arose on account of caste. It may continue to persist even after conversion. One cannot assume that his life has suddenly improved socially and educationally because he renounced the past caste-based social structure and joined the new one. He enjoyed constitutional benefits, which now stop upon conversion because the law does not permit him to claim them.On the one hand, ignoring the social and educational impacts that persist after conversion runs counter to the purpose of social justice. On the other hand, continuing eligibility based on a previous social identity without examining the current situation creates practical problems. Thus, there is a strong friction between social reality and the legal framework of constitutional reservation. Surely, there must be a way to reconcile this. However, the courts are not the appropriate place for such reconciliation. Merely identifying a social problem in court cannot guarantee a new reservation category or classification in the existing scheme. The courts can interpret constitutional provisions, examine the validity of classifications and evaluate state actions, but cannot create a new reservation category. That is a matter of state policy. In fact, Indra Sawhney’s case also emphasised that the authority appointed to identify backwardness must be left to do so.A religious convert should not acquire reservation benefits based on previous social identity or by joining the new community, but on well-founded evidence that they still face social disadvantage. Reservation should never protect one’s past identity; rather, it should lift those disadvantaged in education and employment because of societal inequalities. But if past social disadvantage continues even after conversion, then reservation benefits should be extended to lift those in deprived status. That would be an emphatic way to implement social justice schemes.Mohamed Sajid Nadwi is a practising Advocate at the High Court of Madras.

title: Bengaluru court awards ₹3.78 crore to whistleblower terminated by Willis Towers Watson
summary: A Bengaluru court has awarded nearly ₹3.78 crore in damages to a former Willis Towers Watson (WTW) employee after finding that his termination was retaliatory and breached the company’s obligation to protect whistleblowers [Naveen Kumar Midha Vs Rohit Jain].By way of a judgment dated October 16, Additional City Civil and Sessions Judge Shirin Javeed Ansari partly allowed the suit filed by Naveen Kumar Midha, who had headed the company’s Health and Benefits business.The Court held that a contractual provision permitting termination upon notice or payment of salary could not, by itself, excuse a breach of the company’s commitment against retaliation for being a whistleblower. “The contractual provision permitting termination upon notice or salary in lieu thereof does not, by itself, cure an exercise of that power which is inconsistent with the applicable non-retaliation commitment,” the Court said.Midha alleged that he had raised concerns about fictitious transactions, phantom payments, questionable vendor payments and alleged sub-broking activities contrary to regulatory requirements. He relied on communications and meetings between July 2017 and July 2018 to establish that he had reported these concerns to senior personnel of the company.He was suspended on July 17, 2018. The suspension was revoked on September 27 but his employment was terminated the following day.The company disputed his claims and relied on the contractual termination provisions. They also pointed to his subsequent employment and remuneration to contest his claim for financial loss.The Court held that the notice clause and whistleblower protection operated in different spheres. One prescribed the mechanism for terminating employment, while the other governed the treatment of employees making protected disclosures. Both had to be read harmoniously.It was unnecessary to hold that the whistleblower policy had deleted or superseded the termination clause. The question was whether the termination power had been exercised contrary to an independently binding obligation against retaliation.“The policy is not to be treated as a decorative or inconsequential document. Its legal significance depends upon its proved terms and applicability, but once those matters are established, the Court must give it due effect in determining whether the defendants complied with their obligations,” the Court stated.However, the Court distinguished an internal policy expressing an aspiration from one imposing an enforceable obligation. Its terms, adoption and applicability had to be proved. Here, a defence witness acknowledged that the company had adopted the WTW policies, that the code of conduct was binding and that it protected whistleblowers against retaliation.The Court also distinguished reporting suspected wrongdoing from conclusively proving it. “A whistleblower’s complaint may warrant examination under the applicable policy even where the alleged wrongdoing has not yet been conclusively established,” the Court opined.Whistleblower protection would not necessarily depend on prior proof of every allegation. Nevertheless, the employee has to establish that the disclosure fell within the policy and that the adverse employment action was connected with it.The Court clarified that neither the timing of termination nor the absence of a formal inquiry automatically established illegality against Midha on the part of the company.However, the Court drew its conclusion in favour Midha after taking into account cumulative evidence, including the applicable policy, witness admissions, management’s decision not to pursue the matter underlying Midha’s suspension and his immediate termination without a conclusive finding of misconduct.In light of the above, the Court awarded ₹3,67,97,082 in special damages to Midha and ₹10 lakh for mental agony, payable jointly and severally by four WTW entities. It separately ordered each defendant to pay ₹2 lakh each to Midha for injury to his professional life.It also ordered a fresh, dignified relieving letter and removal of stigmatic observations from his suspension-related records.The Court also directed perjury complaints against Vijay Kumar Suri, Managing Director and Principal Officer of Willis Towers Watson India Insurance Brokers, and Cedric Luah, who headed WTW’s Health and Benefits practice for Asia and Australasia. Both had incorrectly testified as defence witnesses.It clarified that its findings were prima facie and that the Magistrate would independently determine guilt.Midha was represented by advocates Arjuna Rao, who was instructed by advocates Madhav Misra and Ketan Paul of Curiam Legal.Rohit Jain, Vijay Suri and Willis Towers Watson India Insurance Brokers were represented by advocate Syed Shujath Mehdi.Vandana Bhatt, Willis Europe BV, Willis Towers Watson PLC and Willis Towers Watson India Private Limited were represented by advocate Perikal K Arjun of Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas. [Read Judgment]

title: Pre-2019 consumer claims above ₹50 Lakh maintainable before State Commission: J&K High Court
summary: The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court recently ruled that consumer claims exceeding ₹50 lakh are maintainable before the J&K State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission if they were instituted before the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 came into force in the Union Territory [Tabeen Mineral Water Pvt. Ltd. V/s National Insurance Company Limited]A Division Bench of Chief Justice Dr. Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Mohd Yousuf Wani asked the State Commission to re-adjudicate cases it had previously dismissed for lack of pecuniary jurisdiction.“All those cases in which the pecuniary limit is above Rupees Fifty lakhs shall be admissible and shall be required to be adjudicated on merits and any dismissal or non-interference on account of the upper pecuniary limit of Rupees Fifty lakhs is quashed, and such matters shall be required to be re-adjudicated by the Commission strictly in accordance with law and on their own merits,” the Court ordered.Chief Justice Dr. Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Mohd Yousuf WaniThe Court was hearing an appeal and a writ petition concerning consumer complaints filed before the State Consumer Commission.It was submitted that the Commission had dismissed the complaints, which sought compensation exceeding ₹50 lakh, solely on the ground that it lacked the pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain them.In the judgment passed on October 21, the Court examined the legislative history of Section 15 of the Jammu and Kashmir Consumer Protection Act, 1987. The law, which was replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, initially provided for a pecuniary limit of ₹50,000 to ₹10 lakh. In 1997, these limits were increased to ₹5 Lakh and ₹30 Lakh.The Court noted that a 1998 amendment omitted the upper pecuniary limit of ₹30 lakh. It added that a subsequent amendment in 2011 substituted the figures of ₹5 lakh and ₹30 lakh with ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh without addressing the earlier omission.The Court said this omission had led to a legislative anomaly as a person claiming compensation above ₹50 lakh was rendered remediless. It noted that the Commission had been following this position of no upper limit for a number of years until the High Court in Met Life India Insurance Company Ltd & Another v. Abdul Aziz Khan observed that the upper pecuniary limit of ₹50 Lakh was operational.After examining the earlier ruling, the Court said it had "not drawn any conclusion or any kind of precedent oriented mandate to be followed regarding Section 15 of the Act of 1987." Thus, the Court ruled that its decision in Met Life cannot have a binding value. It also observed that a person cannot be rendered remediless for seeking compensation because of a legislative anomaly for the pre-2019 cases. For post-2019 cases, a person can approach the National Commission, it added.Thus, the Court ruled that for all the cases filed before 2019, the upper pecuniary limit shall be unlimited. "This Court, while making a purposive interpretation of the legal position, lays down the law that any case pending prior to the coming into force of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, shall be dealt with, for the purpose of pecuniary jurisdiction, only in terms of the 1998 Gazette Notification, which omitted the upper pecuniary limit of Rupees thirty lakhs," it said.Senior Advocate ZA Qureshi with advocate Rehana Fayaz represented the petitioner in a writ petition. Advocate Irfan Rasool Wani appeared for the appellant in an appealAdvocate NA Dendru appeared for the respondents.[Read Judgment]

title: Kerala High Court changes its internship policy; only those in final 2 years of LL.B allowed
summary: The Kerala High Court has revised its 2026 internship policy, introducing new rules governing applications, entry passes, attendance and the conduct of law students interning at the High Court.The revised policy, titled 'Internship Policy for the High Court of Kerala-2026 (Amended),' was notified on October 17 and lays down detailed procedures governing internships at the High Court. Clause 6(a) of the policy states that "only students in the last two years of their law courses shall be eligible to undergo an internship in the High Court."The restriction, however, does not apply to internships permitted at the discretion of judges.The policy applies to law students interning under High Court judges and other sections of the Court as well as offices including those of the Advocate General, Additional Solicitor General, Director General of Prosecution, Deputy Solicitor General, Kerala State Legal Services Authority, Mediation Centre, Bar Council of Kerala and other advocates.For internship opportunities under the judges, applications will be processed only after obtaining their consent.Under the new framework, students will be required to submit their internship applications through an online module, which will be developed by the High Court. Until the module becomes operational, applications and other internship-related procedures will continue to be handled online.The applications are to be forwarded through the principal or head of the institution where the student is studying. The Public Relations Officer (PRO) of the High Court will be responsible for overseeing the internship program, including processing applications and maintaining attendance records.Interns are prohibited from using mobile phones, cameras or recording devices inside courtrooms. Recording court proceedings in any manner or circulating it on social media to compromise the Court's security would lead to immediate termination of the internship, as per the policy.They are also required to maintain confidentiality and avoid disturbing court proceedings.The interns have to record their attendance daily and the actual number of days where they are physically present in the Court would be counted as the internship period for issuance of internship certificates.[Read Notification]

title: Madhya Pradesh High Court reserves order on Giribala Singh's bail plea in Twisha Sharma death case
summary: The Madhya Pradesh High Court on Monday reserved its order on the bail plea moved by former judicial officer Giribala Singh who is in judicial custody in a case accusing her of subjecting her daughter-in-law Twisha Sharma to cruelty and abetting her suicide. Noida-based Twisha Sharma had married Bhopal-based lawyer Samarth Singh after the two met through a dating app. Barely five months into the marriage, Sharma was found hanging at her matrimonial home in Bhopal on May 12. Justice Ajay Kumar Nirankari heard detailed arguments in Giribala Singh's bail plea since this morning and concluded the hearing around 4:40 pm."Thank you! I will pass the order," the judge said.Justice Ajay Kumar NirankariTwisha Sharma's family have accused her husband and in-laws of subjecting her to persistent domestic violence and harassment over dowry demands, leading to the registration of an FIR at Katara Hills police station under various provisions of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Dowry Prohibition Act.Giribala Singh, former President of the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Madhya Pradesh, was initially granted anticipatory bail by a sessions court. The Madhya Pradesh High Court later cancelled the relief after the State government and the victim's family challenged the order.Meanwhile, the case was transferred to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) which arrested Giribala Singh and Samarth Singh.After their period of CBI custody ended on June 2, a Bhopal court remanded both accused to judicial custody. Their bail petitions are currently pending.Singhs have been charge sheeted by the CBI under Sections 85 (cruelty and harassment caused by husband and his family members) and 108 (abetment to suicide) of the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).The Supreme Court recently stayed the trial in the case while issuing notice to the CBI on a petition moved by the victim's father for transfer of the trial to Delhi.Seeking bail in the matter, Giribala Singh today argued that while she was unhappy with her daughter-in-law's decision to abort her child, she had neither subjected her to cruelty nor abetted her suicide.The Court questioned why she had called various persons in the judiciary and civil administration soon after Twisha Sharma's death. Giribala Singh's counsel said she was trying to convince people that she had not committed any murder as was being alleged. He said there was nothing wrong with informing them about the facts.The counsel also said that there was no allegation of evidence tampering since the day the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) took over the probe. "I am already in custody for five months. I am an old lady of 65. There is no chance of me absconding or tampering with witnesses. Why should now I be detained in judicial custody," he added.Siddharth AgarwalSenior Advocate Siddharth Aggarwal, representing the victim's father, said that an independent and capable woman was reduced to a shadow of herself by the accused.Opposing the bail plea, Aggarwal said Giribala Singh has a propensity to influence the course of investigation. He referred to calls made by her to various persons in positions of power in the judiciary and civil administration soon after Sharma's death."If this is immediate reaction of the person, there can be no doubt that investigative process and the judicial process must be saved from being subverted," Aggarwal said.The senior counsel said Giribala Singh had subjected Sharma to character assassination by questioning her about past relationships. "This is the level to which character assassination of women has become so usual and normal for us. The abuses that this girl had to hear, which are recorded for posterity in those WhatsApp chats and in these statements and in the phone calls are being read out in court today as if it is normal!," Aggarwal said. Aggarwal also referred to the circumstances under which Sharma did not want to conceive a child. In particular, he pointed to the chats indicating that her husband Samarth Singh was using various illicit drugs."This is not a stage where the applicant ought to be released on bail," the senior counsel said.Senior Advocate Sunil JainAdditional Solicitor General Sunil Jain, appearing for CBI, said Giribala Singh was instrumental in instigating cruelty and suicide in the case. "She was a silent spectator but instigated everything. There is sufficient material to demonstrate this," Jain said.He added that Sharma was subjected to cruelty for dowry and character assassinated, prompting her to commit suicide. Jain also submitted that the accused have not been exonerated of the charge of dowry death as the investigation into the offence is still ongoing.

title: Depression after spouse's death sufficient ground to condone delay in consumer complaint: Delhi Commission
summary: The Delhi State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission recently held that depression following the death of a spouse can constitute sufficient cause for excusing delay in filing a consumer complaint [Priya Mehrotra v. Tata AIG General Insurance Co. Ltd.].A Bench of Commission President Justice Sangita Dhingra Sehgal and Member Bimla Kumari made the observation while condoning a 250-day delay in a widow's complaint against Tata AIG General Insurance Company over the rejection of a medical insurance claim.The Commission accepted that the complainant's treatment for clinical depression following her husband's death sufficiently explained the delay."On perusal of record, we find that there has been a delay of 250 days in filing the Complaint before the District Commission, for which, the Appellant has given sufficient cause, being that she was seeking treatment for clinical depression after the demise of her husband. Therefore, it would be in the interest of justice to condone the delay in filing the Complaint of the Appellant. Having condoned the delay, the District Commission is directed to decide the said Complaint on merits." the Commission observed.The case arose after Priya Mehrotra's husband, Saurabh Mehrotra, a dentist, suddenly fell ill while working at his clinic on August 16, 2021.He was initially taken to Kukreja Hospital in Delhi and subsequently referred to Sir Ganga Ram Hospital.According to the complaint, initial investigations did not reveal serious abnormalities. However, his condition deteriorated, and doctors subsequently informed his family that his liver had suffered severe damage.He was later shifted to the Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences, where he died on October 27, 2021.Mehrotra subsequently sought reimbursement of ₹25.73 lakh towards her husband's treatment under a Tata AIG health insurance policy.However, the insurer rejected the claim in January 2022, stating that treatment for cirrhosis fell within the policy's two-year waiting period.After unsuccessful representations to the insurer and the Insurance Ombudsman, Mehrotra approached the District Consumer Commission alleging deficiency in service.On February 2, 2026, the District Commission dismissed her complaint as time-barred.Challenging the decision, Mehrotra submitted that she had suffered severe psychological distress following her husband's death and developed clinical depression requiring prolonged treatment and counselling.The State Commission examined Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which prescribes a two-year limitation period for consumer complaints.The Commission accepted the medical prescriptions produced by Mehrotra and concluded that sufficient cause existed to condone the delay.It consequently set aside the District Commission's order and directed it to decide the complaint on merits within three months of its October 7 judgment.The Commission did not decide whether Tata AIG was justified in rejecting the insurance claim.Mehrotra was represented by Neha Gund & Associates.[Read Judgment]

title: CMRL-Exalogic case: Kerala High Court stays FIR against ex-CM Pinarayi Vijayan, daughter Veena, others
summary: The Kerala High Court on Monday stayed further investigation in a criminal case registered against CPI (M) leader and former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, his daugher Veena Thaikkandiyil, her husband and MLA Mohammed Riyas, and others in connection with the CMRL-Exalogic case [Pinarayi Vijayan v. Adv KM Shajahan & Ors.].A Bench of Justices KM Natarajan and Johnson John passed the interim order on appeals filed by Vijayan and others (appellants) challenging a single-judge's directive to register a first information report (FIR) in the CMRL-Exalogic case. Another Division Bench of the High Court had previously declined to hear their appeals without delving into its merits and dismissed their applications seeking permission to appeal the single-judge order.Subsequently, the appellants moved the Supreme Court for relief. The top court last week said that the Division Bench of the High Court ought to to hear the appeals in detail. The top court, therefore, stayed the probe against the appellants for a week so that the High Court can hear the appeal. Following this development, the High Court heard appeals today and stayed the single-judge ruling. It has also ordered a stay on the investigation in the case until further orders. "All four appeals are hereby admitted. Consequently, the judgment of the single judge of this court under challenge is stayed until the next date of hearing. Further investigation on the FIR is kept in abeyance until further orders," the Court said.Justice K Natarajan and Justice Johnson JohnThe matter is tied to alleged irregularities in the financial transactions between Cochin Minerals and Rutile Limited (CMRL) and Exalogic Solutions Private Limited, a company owned by Veena Thaikkandiyil.The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has claimed that it unearthed certain incriminating material, which it shared with the Kerala Police. The State decided to set up a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to hold a preliminary inquiry instead of immediately registering an FIR.A lawyer named KM Shajahan, who had also served as an additional private secretary to former CM and CPI (M) leader, late VS Achuthanandan when he was the Leader of Opposition, approached the Kerala High Court challenging this move and sought the registration of an FIR.On October 9, a single-judge Bench of the High Court allowed Shajahan's petition and ordered the State's Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) to register an FIR based on the ED's information against Vijayan, Veena, Riyas and others suspected of corruption, including Nikhil P, Hassan Varish, Shyjal Muhammad and Nandulal M.This was challenged before a Division Bench of the High Court by way of appeals filed by Vijayan, Veena, Riyas and others.Notably, the appellants (Vijayan, Veena, Riyas and others) were not parties to the writ petition in which the single-judge's October 9 order was passed. Therefore, a question arose as to whether they can be given permission to challenge a judgment in a case to which they were not parties.A Division Bench of Justice K Natarajan and Justice Johnson John on October 15 refused to permit the appellants to proceed with their appeal. It held that the appellants can still challenge the FIR itself, instead of the single-judge order for the registration of the FIR.Vijayan and others then approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's direction to register an FIR.The vacation bench of the Supreme Court comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took exception to the High Court hastily directing registration of FIR based on EDs information, without hearing Vijayan.The Court also cautioned the ED against meddling into the domain of other probe agencies.Pertinently, the Supreme Court said that the issue of whether a State agency is obligated to register an FIR in a corruption case based on a recommendation made by ED is an issue that needs detailed examination.The matter was then sent back to the High Court's Division Bench for a detailed examination on the merits of the appeals filed by Vijayan and the others. Senior Advocates Siddharth Luthra and Gopalakrishna Kurup appeared today for Pinarayi Vijayan. Senior Advocate N Hariharan appeared for Veena Thaikkandiyil and Mohammed Riyas.During the hearing, the appellants' counsel questioned how an FIR was registered in this case merely on the ED's dictates."ED is an organ of the centre. Direction cannot be given by ED to State Police to register FIR ... Why is the ED piggybacking on the shoulders of this interloper?" contended Hariharan. He highllighted that the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) had already initiated a probe into similar allegations. He termed the ED's move to call for parallel criminal proceedings mischievous, particularly since the SFIO probe has been stayed. "Since SFIO probe has been stayed, the mischief they (ED) have done is to piggyback on the shoulders of the writ petitioner who has no locus in this case."Hariharan also questioned whether there was any prima facie case made out for the FIR to stand."They simply throw words arround like 'quid pro quo'. Allegations should be clear. The money should reach the hands of either Riyas or Vijayan. That is not there."Another argument made was that the single-judge court did not have the jurisdiction to entertain Shajahan's plea for an FIR once it was admitted that the plea appeared to be in the nature of a public interest litigation. The appellants further flagged that they were not heard at all before the single-judge passed an order directing the registration of an FIR against them."I ought to have been a party when the single judge was hearing the third party petitioner," Luthra said. Advocate General Jaju Babu appeared for the State and defended its move to first conduct a preliminary inquiry before deciding whether an FIR was warranted in the matter."Our decision to order a preliminary enquiry after receiving information from ED was correct. That is our position. We did not say we will not register an FIR. This was the first step."Additional Solicitor General of India P Sreekumar represented the ED and maintained that a stay on the SFIO probe into the CMRL case could not be cited by the appellants to challenge the validity of the State Police's FIR. "The challenge against the SFIO probe was made by the company, CMRL. Here, the individuals are before the court," he said. He also urged the Court not to grant any interim stay. Advocate V Sethunath appeared for Shajahan. After hearing the preliminary submissions, the Court has issued an interim stay on the FIR till further orders. Besides Senior Siddharth Luthra, N Hariharan and Gopalakrishna Kurup, advocates Mayank Jain, Ameen Hassan, Gilbert George Correya, Madhur Jain, Arpit Goel, KK Ravindranath, P Narayanan, Manu V, Thanushree Damodaran, Abhijith MA and Clarina Christopher P also appeared for Vijayan and Veena.Riyas, Nikhil, Varish, Shyjal, and Nandulal's appeals were filed through advocates Ameen Hassan K, Lisna Sherin TT, Ummul Fadla T, Abdul Fathah Rajesh A and Muneer Ahmed.
