title: Minority judge blocked, Dhana's tactics, government's pre-approval: Justice SK Kaul reveals inner workings of Collegium
summary: The questionable working of the Supreme Court Collegium - the body responsible for appointing judges to the higher judiciary - has been laid bare by one of its former members and retired Supreme Court Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul.In his memoirs titled Without Fear or Favour, the former judge most startlingly reveals that ex-Chief Justice of India (CJI) DY Chandrachud, as head of the Collegium, would seek the Central government's stance on potential appointments before consulting with the rest of the judges on the Collegium.The Collegium system was preserved by the Supreme Court in a bid to maintain judicial independence, free from executive influence. However, Justice Kaul seems to think that political considerations have long since crept, calling the method into question.In a scathing indictment of the system, he writes,"The collegium system worked well enough in the initial years, but over time, the judges have at times outdone the politicians. I have often been asked whether it is not altogether for the good that politicians have been excluded from the appointments process, and I have always replied to this slightly naive premise that ‘Judges ki rajneeti, rajnitigyon ki rajneeti ko mat kar deti hai. (The politics of the judges outdoes the politics of the politicians themselves.)’."CJI Chandrachud and pre-approval of government for judges' appointmentsJustice Kaul, who has known former CJI Chandrachud for over four decades, said that his relationship with the man he calls 'Dhana' had strained during his final years as a Supreme Court judge. He attributes this to one thing, more than others:"I believed he was too deferential to the government on appointment matters."He prefaces his opinion by saying that he was not one among those who believed that the government should not have any say in judicial appointments. He writes,"Total purdah cannot be the standard for independence, and blockages are bound to occur and do occur when consultation breaks down. But there is a difference between consultation and what I came to regard as pre-approval – seeking the government’s nod before the collegium had even formally deliberated. That sends the wrong signal. Any political class will always assert itself if you give them a wedge in the door. This is not in any sense a partisan matter but simply a question of the inevitable institutional dynamics of power."He also recalls an incident where Justice Chandrachud held court till 9 PM just to avoid a Collegium meeting where the then CJI and other judges were waiting for him for hours together."Although I maintained a good working and personal relationship with him, I considered this an atrocious way to treat the chief justice and one’s colleagues, and I said as much to him in a later encounter when he walked into my chamber after he had been sworn in. After some discussion, I pointed out to him that we were not vella (jobless) to keep waiting for him."Chief Justice of India DY ChandrachudJustice Sanjay Kishan KaulAfter some discussion, I pointed out to Justice Chandrachud that we were not vella (jobless) to keep waiting for him.Justice Kaul goes on to say that the government's tendency to interfere stemmed from the Supreme Court's striking down of the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) in 2015. In that judgment, the Court denied the government's proposal of an NJAC - comprising the Chief Justice of India, the two judges next in seniority, the Union Law Minister and two eminent personalities chosen by a committee of the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice and the Leader of the Opposition - to appoint judges to the Supreme Court and the High Courts."The collegium system had its problems, and the last years of my tenure starkly demonstrated them: the opacity, the concentration of power and the susceptibility to government pressure through informal channels. The political system had not lived down the Supreme Court’s rejection of the NJAC. Even today, I think they have not accepted it. It is one of the reasons for the pressure I witnessed in the form of blockages in clearing names, insistence on pre-approvals and quiet vetoes exercised through the return of files."Justice Sanjay Kishan KaulThere is a difference between consultation and what I came to regard as pre-approval – seeking the government’s nod before the collegium had even formally deliberated. That sends the wrong signal.What they do in the shadows: Collegium functioningJustice Kaul also narrates a few examples of the opacity with which the Collegium functions. In his own case, he was transferred to the Madras High Court, known then to be a 'problematic' High Court not least because of constant clashes between lawyers and police. "To be perfectly frank, the posting was widely perceived, in legal circles in Delhi and beyond, as a punishment posting," he writes.Justice Kaul, then Chief Justice of the Punjab & Haryana High Court for a year-and-a-half, was not keen on being transferred, given his pending work."I sensed that there were other gears turning, about which my interlocutors were not quite being open with me. I felt that perhaps there were others whom the collegium wanted to bring to the Supreme Court and that my being sent to Chennai was a way to forestall my own claim to elevation for some time."He recalls a discussion with then CJI RM Lodha, who asked him for alternatives to be transferred as Chief Justice of the Madras High Court. After the CJI said no to all the names Justice Kaul suggested, the former said, "We think that either you or Dhananjay must go," Justice Kaul writes,"Justice Chandrachud had taken over as the Chief Justice in Allahabad just six months ago. It was obvious that he would not be moved, nor should he have been. I told Justice Lodha, simply, ‘In that case, sir, it looks like it’s my turn'."While in Madras, Justice Kaul says he came across many suitable candidates for elevation that were turned down for bizarre reasons. On Senior Advocate NL Rajah, he recounts a conversation with a former CJI who wasn't even aware that his Collegium turned down Rajah's name."Another capable candidate had been lost to the bench for good. It drove home the point to me of how flawed and opaque the collegium process had become. People in the running for a high constitutional office were being rejected (or sometimes, accepted) for reasons the selectors did not even care to remember."Reference in the book is also made to the stalled elevations of Senior Advocates Saurabh Kirpal and Sanjoy Ghose.Senior Counsel NL RajahThe memoirs also recalls a Dalit district court judge who was competent and honest, but was not considered for elevation because a consultee judge was displeased with him."The consultee judge had visited the district where this officer was posted. He had felt – rightly or wrongly – that the bandobast had been insufficient. On this basis, the consultee judge had recorded an adverse remark, and the collegium, not knowing the background or caring to enquire into the details, had acted on it. It was a grotesque outcome. A man’s career had been curbed not because of any failing in his work or his integrity, but because a visiting judge felt he had not been given enough attention."Minority Judge blockedAnother failed elevation while Justice Kaul was a member of the Collegium concerned a candidate from a minority faith. The government, Justice Kaul reveals, had a bizarre reservation."Officially, the government queried whether additional representation of minority faiths was really required on the court, pointing to certain judges from other religious minorities who were already serving. I was troubled by this logic. ‘We had agreed on this name,’ I said. The judge happened to be from a state that, at that time, was in fact under-represented on the Supreme Court."He added that CJI Chandrachud shared some view which the government had conveyed and it provoked him."Then came a further query, voiced by the chief justice, which I found rather bizarre: The government wanted to know which caste the candidate’s family had belonged to before they converted to another faith. How on earth could we possibly have known that?...The follow-up was chilling: Dhan shared something with me as the government view that I must now redact, but it did provoke me."Justice Sanjay Kishan KaulDhan shared something with me as the government view that I must now redact, but it did provoke me.In another startling revelation, Justice Kaul said that before the tenure of CJI UU Lalit, the Collegium did not follow the practice of analysing the judgments and disposal rate of potential appointees to the Supreme Court."How could we assess a judge’s suitability for the Supreme Court without reading their prominent judgments? I felt that we judges did not appreciate how bizarre it would sound to a member of any other profession that this was not already the case...That elevations were made based on ‘soundings’ and purely informal impressions – just or unjust – that had been formed about a candidate did not sit right with me."On the general functioning of the Collegium - something that is steeped in opacity - Justice Kaul reveals that it is only the CJI who proposes names, which other Collegium members agree or disagree on. A recommendation goes through only if there is a unanimous or a 4:1 agreement; 3:2 agreements do not go through. During his time as a Collegium members, he says, there was largely agreement on candidates.He also reveals what a change in the Collegium composition implies."A candidate who had been favourably viewed by one collegium could be blocked by the next simply because of a personal antipathy or a difference of judicial philosophy in the new member. I had seen this happen repeatedly – a junior judge appointed ahead of a senior, or a senior overlooked entirely, only to be elevated the moment his opponent on the collegium departed. This was perhaps the system’s deepest flaw: the appearance of objectivity masking what were, in many cases, intensely personal decisions."A tribute to Arun JaitleyJustice Kaul further speaks of the increasing friction between the executive and the judiciary over judicial appointments. He said that things got worse after the passing of former Union Law Minister Arun Jaitley, a man he describes as a symbol of a more gentlemanly style of Indian politics. "He was that rare breed: a politician whom judges could not but respect and a lawyer whom politicians could not afford to ignore. In all the time I knew him, including when he was at the apex of his power, he never once even attempted to speak to me about a matter that was before me or to influence me in any way. But if something on the administrative side was going wrong, it could be mentioned to him, and he had the ear of those at the top. He was never vindictive or small, and he believed, as I did, that merit and not ideology should decide appointments. His passing was a real loss, for no comparable face replaced him, and afterwards names began to stick on the smallest of pretexts, as I have recounted above."Arun JaitleyJustice Sanjay Kishan KaulArun Jaitley was never vindictive or small, and he believed, as I did, that merit and not ideology should decide (judicial) appointments.The last of the 'liberal' judgesJustice Kaul narrates a story where he and other Supreme Court judges were invited to a dinner at CJI Chandrachud's residence."...my family and I were invited, and so were Justices Hrishikesh Roy, Rajiv Shakdher and Deepak Gupta...After it, he (Chandrachud) gave his post-dinner speech, and in the speech, he said that we had here, himself included, some of the last of the liberal judges. That is to say, liberalism not in terms of any political commitment but an overall broad-minded approach. I listened to it, and after the dinner I said to him, ‘See, you mentioned this fact. Now, what did we do to get more liberal judges to the Supreme Court?’ I don’t think any of us could have had a very good answer to my question."

title: Husband forcing wife to accept extramarital affair and live with mistress is mental cruelty: Jharkhand High Court
summary: A husband’s insistence that his wife must live alongside the woman with whom he is having an extramarital affair will amount to mental cruelty of the highest degree, the Jharkhand High Court recently observed while dissolving a marriage that had remained broken since 2019.A Division Bench of Justices Sujit Narayan Prasad and Pradeep Kumar Srivastava held that the husband compelling the wife to accept his affair with another woman under the guise of a "younger sister" shatters matrimonial trust irreparably.Hence, it allowed the appeal filed by the wife, a medical practitioner, challenging a November 2023 order of a family court at Hazaribagh which had dismissed her divorce petition filed under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.The High Court held that the family court had appreciated the evidence in a piecemeal manner and overlooked the principle of preponderance of probabilities applicable to matrimonial proceedings."Marriage is a relationship built on mutual trust, companionship and shared experiences. Relationship of wife and husband is based on the trust and respect to have upon each other and if it is broken it is non-repairable as the trust is the foundation of marriage," the Court observed.The parties, both doctors, married in February, 2018, and lived in Dhanbad. While the husband was posted at Primary Health Centre in Tundi, the wife was employed with Bharat Coking Coal Limited (BCCL). They began living separately in September 2019.Justice Sujit Narayan Prasad and Justice Pradeep Kumar Srivastava The wife alleged that the husband entered into an extramarital relationship with a widow. Though the husband had executed a written bond during a family intervention undertaking to cease contact, he continued the relationship. When the wife protested, she was subjected to physical assaults with household implements like a broom and a mop stick, causing medical complications, including a slip-disc and traumatic osteoarthritis.The husband denied the allegations and claimed the medical prescriptions from a clinic owned by the wife's father were fabricated. He had also previously obtained an ex-parte decree for restitution of conjugal rights in January 2023.The High Court held that the medical documents could not be brushed aside merely because they emanated from the clinic of the wife's father. It further observed that the husband's conduct compelled the wife to leave her matrimonial home.Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Samar Ghosh v. Jaya Ghosh, the Bench noted that prolonged separation since 2019 itself established that the marital bond was irreparably damaged.Accordingly, the Court dissolved the marriage and granted liberty to the wife to seek permanent alimony under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act before the Family Court.Advocates Abhishek Thakur and Pratyush Navneet represented the appellant-wife. Advocate Soumitra Baroi appeared for the respondent-husband.

title: Non-Hindus can't enter Agamic temples without giving undertaking that they believe in the deity: Madras High Court
summary: The Madras High Court recently ruled that non-Hindus cannot enter Agamic temples in Tamil Nadu without affirming their reverence for the presiding deity and agreeing to follow the customs and practices of the temple [Thangam Venkatesh Vs State of TN].A Division Bench of Justices GR Swaminathan and P Murugan held that non-Hindus who fail to furnish such an undertaking affirming their reverence for the temple's deity cannot enter the temple. "Even entry into the temple premises, cannot be permitted for non-Hindus who sport their religious markers and who do not subscribe their reverence for the deity concerned. This subscription (undertaking) must be in the format prescribed by the institution concerned," the Court's October 23 judgment states. Justice GR Swaminathan, Justice P Murugan Madras High CourtEntry into the temple cannot be permitted for non-Hindus who sport their religious markers and who do not subscribe their reverence for the deityThe Court clarified that this ruling is confined to Agamic temples (Hindu temples whose construction, rituals, and worship follow the rules prescribed in the Agamas or traditional Hindu scriptures). The Court contrasted such temples with institutions associated with Lord Ayyappa and Shirdi Sai Baba, which attracted devotees across religious communities."Lord Ayyapa has devotees cutting across religions. Shirdi Sai Baba is also beyond religion. Both Hindus as well as Muslims claimed him as their own. Of course now, he is more a part of the Hindu pantheon," it observed. The Bench also clarified that temple entry restrictions historically imposed on certain Hindu castes under Agamic practices could no longer withstand constitutional scrutiny."Constitution ranks paramount and such regressive theological injunctions have to necessarily give way," the Court held.However, the same cannot be said of non-Hindus, it added. "We hasten to add that those injunctions (temple entry restrictions) will hold good in respect of non-Hindus who do not sign the undertaking," the Court said. The Court was hearing a petition filed by Thangam Venkatesh seeking the enforcement of the Tamil Nadu Temple Entry Authorisation Act, 1947, and the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.The petitioner sought action against individuals allegedly violating temple entry restrictions and the establishment of mechanisms to prevent unauthorised entry into restricted sanctums and mandapams.By its October 23 ruling, the Court agreed with the petitioner. "The petitioner herein is a Hindu. He is entitled to insist that the trustees of the various Agamic temples in Tamil Nadu uphold the Agamic injunctions by not permitting non-Hindus who do not sign the undertaking from crossing the flag-pole. If such entry is permitted, it would defile the sanctity of the temple," it held. The Bench also noted that earlier rulings of the High Court had already addressed the question of non-Hindu entry into temples. However, it considered an authoritative pronouncement necessary in view of certain recent incidents. In this regard, the Court referred to instances involving political leaders entering temples without adhering to prescribed requirements. It specifically referred to Badrudeen Mustafa, an MLA representing Madurai Central, who had entered the Meenakshi temple premises and climbed its towers during Kumbabishekam (temple consecration ceremony)."He claimed that he had a right to inspect if proper amenities are being provided. He also went up the temple towers on the occasion of Kumbabishekam. It is ironical that the said MLA proclaimed that Sanatana Dharma ought to be eradicated," the Court said. The Bench also took judicial notice of an incident involving a Christian minister entering the Thiruchendur temple without furnishing the undertaking required of non-Hindus.In contrast, the Court noted that Chief Minister Joseph Vijay, despite being Christian, gave the undertaking before entering a Meenakshi temple. "We have the illustrious instance of the Hon'ble Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu Shri Joseph Vijay who worshipped Goddess Meenakshi after signing the undertaking. The Hon'ble Chief Minister who is a Christian by faith was not asked to convert to Hinduism. He was only requested to affirm his reverence for the deity. This is what we call as an inclusive approach," the Court said. Madras High CourtCM Joseph Vijay worshipped Goddess Meenakshi ... (he) is a Christian by faith (but) was not asked to convert to Hinduism... (he was) only requested to affirm his reverence for the deity. This is what we call an inclusive approachThe Court went on to note that when politicians enter temples, their sycophants often try to accompany them. While discussing this tendency, the Court took critical note of a video that showed people "wearing skull caps" pushing their way into a Hindu temple's premises, despite opposition from temple devotees."We take judicial notice of a video doing rounds in the social media of persons wearing skull caps, pushing their way through in Thiruvannamali Arunachaleswarar temple, notwithstanding the vigorous protests of the devotees. The HR&CE staff stood as mute spectators," the Court lamented. The Court criticised such lapses, as well as the tendency of politicians to visit Hindu temples only to "play to the gallery" and garner votes. "We hold that usages and customs of temple cannot kneel down before such display of Chamchagiri and optics," it said. Madras High CourtUsages and customs of temple cannot kneel down before such display of Chamchagiri and optics.The Bench also disagreed with a part of the reasoning in a 1972 Madras High Court judgment that struck down a rule permitting the unrestricted entry of non-Hindus to temples. In the said ruling, the Court had also suggested that no disturbances, including through music and processions, be permitted near mosques. In the October 23 judgment, the High Court expressed that no such restrictions on processions should be put in place, whether it is passing by a mosque, church or temple. "The right of the other communities and religionists to take their processions cannot be curtailed by citing the situs of mosques and churches. Likewise, Hindus also cannot prevent the other religionists from taking their processions in the customary manner on the ground that they pass in front of temples," it held.Advocate G Aravinthsamy appeared for the petitioner.Additional Advocate General PV Balasubramanian, assisted by Government Pleader M P Senthil, appeared for the State authorities.[Read Judgment]

title: Bombay High Court grants relief to actor Imran Khan in challenge to FRRO's leave India notice
summary: The Bombay High Court on Tuesday directed that an October 14 notice from the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) directing actor Imran Khan to leave India by October 28 (tomorrow) be kept on hold till November 2 [Imran Khan Pal v. Union of India & Ors].A Division Bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna briefly heard the matter today, when the Central government's counsel urged the Court to adjourn the case till November 2, Monday. The Additional Solicitor General (ASG) representing the Centre also assured the Court that no coercive action will be taken against Khan till then."Lordship may keep it on Monday," the ASG said. "But I have to leave tomorrow (according to the FRRO directive)," replied Senior Advocate Venkatesh Dhond, representing Khan. "(Court) may keep it on Monday. Nothing will happen. That is an oral assurance," the ASG added. The Court, in turn, agreed to adjourn the case and added that the FRRO's order be kept on hold till then. "ASG seeks time. Matter stands over to November 2 at 3 pm. The order under challenge shall be kept in abeyance till the next date," the Court said. Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait SethnaKhan has petitioned the Court on October 17 to quash the October 14 "Leave India Notice" issued by the FRRO. He also sought an interim stay on deportation, lookout notices, and interference with his Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) status.The October 14 directive followed his brief police detention after participating in protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and a complaint filed by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya for alleged public-order infractions.Khan argued that he received the FRRO notice solely for attempting to attend the protest.In his plea, Khan contended that executive authorities acted with unusual haste and without prior hearing, bypassing his statutory rights due to pressure from political social media campaigns rather than independent reasoning. He claimed the FRRO circumvented Section 7D of the Citizenship Act, which mandates a formal show-cause notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard before revoking OCI residency.Meanwhile, on October 17, the FRRO proceeded to issue a show-cause notice as well under Section 7D regarding OCI cancellation. This specific notice, however, has not been challenged in Khan's current petition.Khan has also requested the production of all internal records related to the decision.Khan was represented by advocates Zulfiquar Memon, Parvez Memon and Chirag Naik from MZM Legal.[Live Coverage]Bombay High Court to shortly begin hearing the plea by Bollywood actor Imran Khan challenging the “Leave India Notice” issued by FRRO mandating him to leave by October 28, tomorrow. @ImranKhanActor #BombayHighCourt #ImranKhan pic.twitter.com/AXiNgpu1gV— Bar and Bench (@barandbench) October 27, 2026

title: Supreme Court stays P&H High Court order barring Rohtak judges from hearing bail pleas in DHL fraud case
summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday stayed a Punjab and Haryana High Court order that had restrained judges posted in Rohtak from dealing with bail petitions arising out a criminal case against DHL Infratech Pvt Limited and Gupta Property Developers [Sidhant Ohlan v. State of Haryana].A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran issued notice and stayed the operation of the order passed by the High Court on September 30. "Issue notice. In the meantime, there shall be a stay of the operation of the impugned order," the Bench directed.Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice Vinod ChandranThe order under challenge was passed by the High Court while hearing an anticipatory bail plea filed by Subhash Gupta, a director of Gupta Property Developers Limited. The case concerns allegations of cheating against DHL Infratech Pvt Limited and Gupta Property Developers, which had induced several homebuyers to invest in their residential project 'DHL New Town' in Sector-27A, Rohtak.According to the complainants, despite payment of consideration amounts, neither possession of the units was delivered nor were sale deeds executed. Preliminary police inquiries had revealed that nearly ₹11.69 crore belonging to at least 30 buyers was involved in the alleged scam.While considering the bail plea, the High Court had expressed strong displeasure over the conduct of the local judiciary and police. It noted that several co-accused, including directors of DHL Infratech, were granted bail by the trial court in Rohtak despite their alleged involvement in other financial scams.Hence, it had restrained judicial officers posted at Sessions Division in Rohtak from hearing any bail applications connected to the case.The High Court had further observed that police officials posted at Rohtak were shielding the real culprits and hesitating to take action against the developers even months after the registration of the FIR. Therefore, it had asked the Haryana government to appoint a senior IPS officer to probe the matter.Aggrieved by the blanket restraint placed on the trial judges in Rohtak, a petition was moved before the apex court challenging the High Court’s directions.Senior Advocate K Parameshwar along with advocates Amit Dwivedi, Gaurav Arya, Sai Kaushal, and Aman Verma appeared for the petitioner. title: AP municipal polls: Supreme Court moots broad guidelines but says can't order roving inquiry into YSRCP's allegations
summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday orally remarked that it could not order a fishing or roving inquiry into allegations that candidates belonging to the YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) were prevented from filing nominations for local body elections in Andhra Pradesh.A Bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana observed that allegations of wrongful exclusion involve disputed questions of fact which could not be adjudicated in the ongoing proceedings."We will not order a fishing or roving inquiry. We will issue a set of guidelines so that it can be followed," CJI Surya Kant said.However, the Court said it will consider laying down guidelines to safeguard the electoral process including preservation of CCTV footage.Justice Joymalya Bagchi, CJI Surya Kant and Justice V MohanaThe Court was examining compliance with its earlier directions requiring the State Election Commission (SEC) to consider complaints of candidates allegedly prevented from filing nominations.YSRCP approached the Supreme Court after the Andhra Pradesh High Court declined relief concerning nomination arrangements and extension of deadlines.The party alleged violence and intimidation in several places, including Kadapa, Tirupati, Punganur and Rayachoti.On October 21, a vacation Bench of Justices Bagchi and Mohana directed the SEC to consider representations, including electronic evidence, and extend nomination deadlines wherever candidates were found to have been prevented from filing nominations due to law and order problems.The Commission was also directed to defer publication of the final list of candidates until October 25.When the matter was taken up for hearing today, the Bench noted that the SEC had acted upon representations and extended nomination deadlines in certain cases.It said candidates claiming wrongful exclusion would have to establish that they had attempted to file nominations but were prevented from doing so."These are disputed questions of fact," the Bench observed.Senior Advocate Maninder Singh, appearing for YSCRP, submitted that a large number of candidates had been excluded despite approaching the authorities. He also referred to allegations concerning approximately 1,200 candidates in other local body elections.However, the Bench said it could not examine such allegations individually during the ongoing electoral process."We cannot go into this nebulous area," the Court remarked, while clarifying that aggrieved candidates could pursue remedies through election petitions.Senior Advocate Siddharth Luthra, appearing for the State government, opposed further intervention by the Court. He argued that opening individual grievances would create uncertainty in the electoral process.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta also expressed concern over repeated applications concerning the elections.The Bench mooted preservation of CCTV recordings to enable examination of electoral grievances at an appropriate stage.Maninder Singh sought directions akin to what had been passed in relation to Punjab polls. "In the Punjab case, Your Lordships appointed a judge and passed directions.The facts here require even more serious consideration. Of approximately 1,600 candidates in the second phase of elections under the same notification, including Zilla Parishad elections, 1,200 were allegedly prevented from filing nominations. Please consider adopting the mechanism followed in the Punjab case," Singh said. "The facts of the Punjab case were different," Luhtra rebutted.The CJI eventually indicated that comprehensive guidelines would be issued to safeguard the electoral process, while distinguishing earlier judicial interventions made in exceptional circumstances.It then proceeded to defer the case for three weeks.[Read Live Coverage][YSRCP vs State of AP] Supreme Court says allegations that candidates were prevented from filing nominations in Andhra Pradesh local body elections involve disputed questions of fact that cannot be adjudicated at this stage.The Bench notes that the State Election Commission has… pic.twitter.com/pi2Ewgbna2— Bar and Bench (@barandbench) October 27, 2026

title: Bombay High Court quashes FIR against B.Tech student for Instagram repost on Operation Sindoor
summary: The Bombay High Court on Tuesday quashed a criminal case against an engineering student for a social media post which allegedly contradicted Government of India’s position on 'Operation Sindoor, the military operation against Pakistan [Khadeejah Shahabuddin Shaikh v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.]Justice Milind N Jadhav observed that the allegations in the First Information Report (FIR) did not disclose the intent of commission of the offences alleged against her."It is seen that the prosecution appears to proceed substantially on the act of re-posting the content without disclosing sufficient particulars establishing the requisite criminal intention or the other essential ingredients of the provisions invoked," the Court said.It added that the accused had corrected herself by voluntarily deleting the re-post and tendering an apology. “A youthful error of judgment cannot automatically be equated with a deliberate criminal act in the absence of material establishing the ingredients of the alleged offences,” the Court further said. Justice Milind JadhavConsidering the accused's young age and career prospects, the Court noted the trauma she had suffered due to her arrest.“Applicant (Shaikh) has already suffered custody. That in itself for a young student is a scar which cannot be erased easily. The prosecution in case is dependent upon mere act of re-posting and nothing more with regard to the incident in question,” it observed. The accused, Khadeejah Shaikh, had re-posted contentious content on Instagram regarding the India-Pakistan conflict on May 7, 2025. However, she voluntarily deleted it within two hours and issued a public apology. Despite her corrective actions, she was arrested two days later for allegedly promoting communal enmity.However, the Court quashed the criminal proceedings, observing that Shaikh was not the original author of the post. It noted that no actual incident of communal disturbance or any other unlawful activity had taken place as a result of Shaikh's re-post. The Court also said that the criminal law cannot be set into motion merely because a particular post is perceived to be offensive, unless the conduct falls within the prohibition prescribed by law.“The mere possibility that a publication may cause displeasure or resentment cannot, by itself, constitute sufficient ground for criminal prosecution,” it added.Advocates Farhana Shah, Omar Shah and Amna Khan appeared for Shaikh. Additional Public Prosecutor Amit A Palkar appeared for State of Maharashtra.[Read Judgment]

title: Delhi High Court upholds 7-year jail term for 5 men convicted in Delhi riots case
summary: The Delhi High Court on Tuesday upheld the trial court order sentencing five men to seven years' imprisonment for culpable homicide over the death of a 22-year-old man during the 2020 Delhi riots. Justice Madhu Jain dismissed the appeal filed by convicts Aman Kashyap, Devinder Kumar, Pradeep Rai, Ashish @ Goli and Arun Kumar against their conviction. The High Court ruled that the evidence showed “more than the mere presence” of the appellants in a crowd.“The common judgment of conviction dated 30.11.2024 and order on sentence dated 13.01.2025 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-03, North-East District, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi, in Sessions Case No. 199/2021, arising out of FIR No. 87/2020 registered at Police Station Dayalpur, are upheld insofar as the present appellants are concerned,” Justice Jain concluded. Justice Madhu Jain The five men were convicted by the trial court under Sections 148 (rioting while armed with a deadly weapon) and 304 Part I (culpable homicide) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Notably, the case arose from an FIR registered at the Dayalpur police station after a man, identified as Monish, was allegedly chased and assaulted by a mob near Brijpuri on February 25, 2020. Monish later died in the hospital. The convicts argued that the prosecution's case suffered from inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts, delays in recording police witnesses' statements and the absence of a test identification parade.Rejecting the challenge, the High Court relied on the testimony of a police constable who identified the five men as being at the forefront of the armed mob and allegedly exhorting others to assault Monish. The court also considered the accounts of other police personnel who described the pursuit and assault before the injured man was rescued.It observed that the absence of a test identification parade did not automatically invalidate identification evidence.Advocates Faraz Anees and Kartik Vashisht appeared for the convicts. title: Delhi High Court slams tax officer for ₹3.91 crore IT demand against security guard with EWS certificate
summary: The Delhi High Court recently quashed a ₹3.91 crore income tax demand against a security guard and cook, strongly criticising the Assessing Officer (AO) for failing to apply his mind in the case [Lalit Vs Union of India]A division bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Aditi Choudhary found that the officer had arbitrarily attributed transactions worth nearly ₹50 crore to the petitioner without looking into his claim that his Permanent Account Number (PAN) had been misused.The Court was particularly critical of the officer's failure to understand the nature of the transactions. "This approach of the AO reveals that he has not even cared to understand the nature of transaction –either he did not understand the basics of accounting or he did not want to," the bench said.Justice Dinesh Mehta and Justice Aditi ChoudharyThe petitioner, Lalit, worked as a contractual security guard and cook at Ashoka Hotel and Vigyan Bhawan in Delhi between 2015 and 2019.He claimed to have obtained a PAN card merely as government-issued identity proof despite having no taxable income.In February 2024, he received a notice alleging cash transactions involving Montage Enterprises Private Limited, a packaging materials company.The notice referred to cash payments of ₹24.86 crore and cash sales of ₹24.62 crore against his PAN.Lalit denied undertaking these transactions and filed complaints with the police and cyber cell, alleging identity theft.However, the AO treated both transactions as his turnover of ₹49.48 crore and assessed 8% as taxable income, resulting in a demand of approximately ₹3.91 crore.The Court found that the officer had effectively counted the same transaction twice by adding the gross amount and the net amount remaining after tax collection.It also noted that no independent inquiry had been conducted to establish Lalit's connection with Montage Enterprises.The Court observed that Lalit had produced bank statements and explained that he had withdrawn provident fund money to meet financial needs. He had also obtained an Economically Weaker Section (EWS) certificate and sought a school fee waiver for his children.The bench said these circumstances warranted empathy and objective scrutiny. It rejected the Income Tax Department's argument that Lalit should pursue the statutory appellate remedy.It noted that securing interim protection ordinarily requires depositing 20 percent of the disputed demand, amounting to nearly ₹78 lakh in the present case.Delhi High CourtA Tax Enforcement Officer should strive to achieve high revenue target but he should keep his feet firmly grounded on the floor of reality.The bench observed that such an enormous demand could threaten the mental and emotional well-being of a financially vulnerable person, implicating Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.It stressed that tax officers should not ignore reality while looking to achieve their revenue targets."A Tax Enforcement Officer should strive to achieve high revenue target but he should keep his feet firmly grounded on the floor of reality. His eyes should be sharp to pierce through the fraud but they should not slip away from the facts"Accordingly, the Court set aside the assessment order dated March 17, 2025. However, it permitted fresh proceedings if credible evidence connecting Lalit to the transactions emerges, subject to statutory limitation.Advocate AK Babbar represented the petitioner.Senior Standing Counsel Gaurav Gupta along with advocates Shivendra Singh, Yojit Pareek, Vedansh Anand and Shivam Kumar, appeared for the respondents.[Read Judgment]

title: Delhi SIR: Why is ECI forcing excluded voters to submit Form 6 as first-time voters? Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday asked the Election Commission of India (ECI) why voters enrolled in earlier voter lists but left out from the draft of the revised voter list being prepared as part of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Delhi, are being compelled to submit Form 6 meant to for the registration of first-time voters.A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a plea alleging lack of transparency in notices issued to voters by election authorities in Delhi during SIR.“Form 6 is for someone seeking enrolment for the first time. Form 8 is for the correction or shifting of residence. Suppose a person was enrolled in Vasant Kunj and has now shifted to Sarita Vihar. That person can disclose the earlier polling booth, electoral roll particulars and voter number, and provide the new address. Why should that person be required to submit Form 6?” CJI Kant asked the ECI today. Justice Bagchi also agreed that issuing Form 6 to a person already enrolled in an earlier voter list may be an erroneous approach. “Why should someone who was already enrolled in the electoral roll be required to submit Form 6? Form 6 is meant for someone seeking enrolment for the first time,” the Bench added. Justice Bagchi went on to observe that the right to vote is a crucial right that cannot be taken away lightly. “The right to vote is a vital right. Your (ECI) exercise must be conducted with due diligence. Suppose a voter was lax and did not respond. Does that mean he forfeits his right forever? A voter may have been unable to respond for various reasons. His name is now missing from the draft roll. He approaches the authorities with his documents, but you insist that he submit Form 6... How does he submit Form 6 when he was already enrolled? There is a structural incongruity which needs to be addressed,” said Justice Bagchi.CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V MohanaThe Court further suggested that it is not sufficient to classify excluded voters under the categories of either shifted or absent. A residual category could be introduced for voters who fail to submit the SIR enumeration form for other reasons, it said. “There may be a residual category of electors who could not respond because the form was not served or for other reasons. Such a person could be permitted to explain the reason for non-response and furnish the necessary documents ... If the authorities are satisfied, his name can be included. If they are not satisfied, they can give reasons, which he can challenge,” the Court said.Supreme CourtThe right to vote is a vital right. Your (ECI) exercise must be conducted with due diligence.The petitioner’s counsel, advocate Prashant Bhushan, told the Court that approximately 43 lakh people have been excluded from the draft voter list on the ground that they had either shifted residence or were absent. Such voters were not added because they failed to submit enumeration forms. Bhushan added that many such voters have claimed that they were unaware that they had to submit these forms. Enumeration forms were sent to outdated addresses, he claimed. He added that these voters were also enrolled in previous voter lists. Despite this, they were now being asked to submit Form 6 if they wished to be included in the revised voter rolls, Bhushan said. Bhushan argued that compelling such voters to submit Form 6 will amount to forcing them to make a false declaration that they have never voted till now.“There is a very simple solution. Allow people who could not submit enumeration forms earlier to submit them even now. Those who have shifted should be permitted to submit an enumeration form along with Form 8. Form 8 is meant for shifted voters. Form 6 is meant for new voters. These are not new voters,” he added. ECIThe SIR is being conducted after more than two decades. We have been evolving methods to ensure that no eligible voter is excluded.Representing the ECI, Senior Advocate Dama Seshadri Naidu replied that the SIR is an evolving process and assured that steps are being taken to address the concerns raised by the petitioner. “There is no question of permanent exclusion. Even after publication of the final roll, an elector can approach the authorities and seek inclusion. Applications can be made until the relevant nomination deadline. The SIR is being conducted after more than two decades. We have been evolving methods, including from our experience in Bihar, to ensure that no eligible voter is excluded,” he said. On the mandate issued to excluded voters to submit Form 6, he added,“When we say first-time inclusion, we mean inclusion afresh in the roll prepared through the SIR exercise. It is a clean-slate exercise. No prosecution has arisen merely because someone used Form 6 in this process.”The Court, meanwhile, questioned why the ECI could not simply allow those who failed to submit enumeration forms on time to send in the same belatedly, instead of asking them to submit Form 6 or any other form.Such an option could be made available until the final voter list is published, the Court suggested. “You have prescribed a cutoff date. Beyond that date, you say the enumeration form cannot be accepted because the draft roll has been published. But until the final roll is prepared, why should an elector who was previously registered be required to submit Form 6? Why can't the enumeration form itself be accepted? … Why should the same form become unacceptable merely because the deadline has passed? You can accept it belatedly and remove the entire difficulty,” the Court said. The Court also urged the ECI to widely publicise the ongoing SIR exercise in simple language, to reduce the number of excluded voters. It said that the list of excluded voters must also be published widely, so that they can take remedial steps.“Make sure the lists are published in the simplest possible language. Inform people that their names appeared in the earlier electoral roll, but the authorities have not been able to contact them or receive their enumeration forms. Explain the consequences if they do not respond. Tell them that wherever they are presently residing, they can approach the nearest electoral authority and submit their forms,” the CJI said. The Court said it would hear the case next after two weeks. Bhushan, meanwhile, pointed out that the deadline for excluded voters to submit Form 6 falls on October 30. “These two weeks will take us beyond that deadline,” he said. Naidu, in turn, assured that the deadline will be extended if necessary.“We will not allow the purpose of the exercise to be defeated. If necessary, we will extend the deadline. We will ensure that,” he said. title: Move Supreme Court: Delhi High Court to advocate seeking ₹50 crore compensation from CJP for disruption
summary: The Delhi High Court on Wednesday asked an advocate to approach the Supreme Court with his plea seeking directions to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) to deposit ₹50 crore as interim compensation for the alleged inconvenience and disruption caused to residents of the national capital by its protests.A Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma noted that the Supreme Court is already seized of similar issues. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta also said that the apex court is dealing with similar matters. Therefore, the Court told the petitioner, advocate Rakesh Kumar Saini, that he should approach the top court. "The judicial discipline warrants that, in such an eventuality, this court must stay its hands away from the proceedings and should not pass conflicting orders," the High Court said in its order.It then disposed of the public interest litigation (PIL). Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre, Justice Sanjay SharmaSaini had filed a PIL in the High Court seeking directions to the Central government and other authorities to initiate proceedings against the CJP. He sought imposition of a collective or community fine and compensation for affected members of the public.He alleged that the CJP and its associates violated conditions imposed on protests at Jantar Mantar, resulting in traffic congestion, disruption of daily activities and inconvenience to traders, commuters, office-goers and schoolchildren.According to the petition, the party was initially permitted to hold a protest against alleged examination paper leaks and the Union Education Minister, but continued occupying the protest site beyond the permitted period. It further alleges that subsequent protest activities, including demonstrations seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, caused disruption in central Delhi.The petition also sought the appointment of a high-powered committee to invite compensation claims from affected citizens and determine the amounts payable. Solicitor General (SG) Tushar Mehta, Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma and Central Government Standing Counsel (CGSC) Premtosh Mishra appeared for the Central government.
